claims.text: Replacing an inert support with an electronically interactive support such as TiO2 will induce charge transfer involving the transition-metal catalyst.
Support-induced charge transfer will shift the metal d-band center.
A shifted d-band center will optimize the binding energies of reaction intermediates.
Optimized intermediate binding will enhance catalytic activity.
Optimized intermediate binding will enhance catalytic selectivity.
Optimized intermediate binding will enhance catalytic durability.
Transition-metal nanoparticles on an inert support such as carbon undergo minimal support-induced charge transfer.
Particle size and dispersion should be matched while temperature, pressure, and reactant concentration are held identical to isolate support effects.
Charge transfer at a metal-TiO2 interface will produce a measurable d-band-center shift.
Intermediate binding that is too strong can cause poisoning, whereas binding that is too weak can impede reactant activation.
TiO2-supported catalysts will show a statistically significant d-band-center shift relative to otherwise comparable carbon-supported catalysts.
The d-band-center shift can be assessed using X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy or DFT calculations.
TiO2-supported catalysts will exhibit improved turnover frequency or reaction rate relative to the inert-support baseline.
TiO2-supported catalysts will exhibit improved product selectivity relative to the inert-support baseline.
TiO2-supported catalysts will exhibit increased durability relative to the inert-support baseline.
The hypothesis is limited to reactions whose performance is sensitive to d-band modulation and adsorption of key intermediates.
The hypothesis applies only when reaction conditions do not cause major structural alteration of the nanoparticles.
The magnitude and direction of an electronic shift can vary with metal identity, composition, and support properties.
Particle size and dispersion can compete with or confound the proposed electronic support effect.
Failure to observe either a statistically significant d-band shift or the predicted performance improvements would falsify the hypothesis.
